items.area_name: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
items.group_name: Individual compliance and tax planning for gross income, AGI, taxable income and estimated taxes
items.task: Consider the impact to an individual's taxable income for certain items of gross income, including imputed interest on below-market rate loan and compensation earned while employed outside the U.S.
items.stem: Hugo Brandt, single, bought a house on January 1, 2018 for $400,000 and rented it to tenants for exactly 48 months. On January 1, 2022 he moved in and has lived there as his main home since. He claimed $48,000 of depreciation during the rental period. He can sell the house on December 31, 2026 (owned 108 months) or keep living in it and sell on December 31, 2028 (owned 132 months). Either sale would bring a net amount realized of $700,000, and there are no other basis changes. How much less taxable gain does Hugo recognize by waiting until 2028?
items.rule_line: Gain on a home sale allocated to periods of nonqualified use, such as rental use before it became the main home, is not excludable, and gain equal to depreciation claimed after May 6, 1997 is also not excludable.

why.A: The depreciation gain of $48,000 is taxable either way. The remaining $300,000 of gain is allocated to nonqualified use (the 48 rental months before he moved in) by months owned: 48/108 in 2026 and 48/132 in 2028. The gain that is allocated to home use is under the $250,000 exclusion in both years, so only the allocation changes: $300,000 x (48/108 - 48/132) = $24,242.
why.B: Allocates the entire $348,000 of gain by months. The $48,000 of gain from depreciation is taxable in full and is taken out before the nonqualified use allocation, so it cannot be spread by months.
why.C: This is the nonqualified use gain if he sells in 2026, not the reduction from waiting. The 2028 sale also has an allocation ($109,091), so only the difference in the two allocations is saved.
why.D: This is his total taxable gain if he sells in 2026 (allocated gain plus the depreciation). Waiting does not remove that, it only reduces the allocated part.

steps: Depreciation gain of 48,000 is not excludable; remaining gain = 348,000 - 48,000 = 300,000
Nonqualified fraction: 48/108 for a 2026 sale and 48/132 for a 2028 sale
Gain allocated to qualified use (166,667 or 190,909) is below the 250,000 exclusion, so difference = 133,333 - 109,091 = 24,242
items.law_note: Nonqualified use excludes any period after the last date the home was used as a main home, and periods before 2009. Rental use from 2018 to 2021 precedes the move-in, so it counts. Confirmed 2026-09-29 (Cornell LII 26 USC 121): (b)(5)(D) applies the nonqualified use allocation after (d)(6), so depreciation gain is removed first; rental use before the move-in counts as nonqualified use.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Gross income items / Analysis

guide.ask: Which part of the gain is taxable no matter when he sells?
guide.reveal: The $48,000 of gain equal to depreciation claimed.

guide.ask: How is the remaining $300,000 split between rental use and home use?
guide.reveal: By months owned: rental months 48 over 108 in 2026, or 48 over 132 in 2028.

guide.ask: Compute the difference.
guide.reveal: $300,000 x (48/108 - 48/132) = $133,333 - $109,091 = $24,242, since the home-use part is under the $250,000 exclusion either way.

items.area_name: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
items.group_name: Individual compliance and tax planning for gross income, AGI, taxable income and estimated taxes
items.task: Consider the impact of using either itemized deductions or the standard deduction for planning purposes given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Ravi and Meera Kapoor file jointly and itemize deductions. Assume that for 2026 the deduction for state and local taxes is capped at $40,400, reduced by 30% of modified AGI above $505,000, and never reduced below $10,000. They paid $48,000 of state income and property taxes. Their modified AGI is $565,000 before any additional retirement deferral. Ravi can defer another $20,000 of salary into his employer's traditional 401(k) plan, which lowers modified AGI dollar for dollar. Assume their marginal rate is 35% throughout, they itemize either way, and no other item changes. By how much does the additional deferral reduce their 2026 federal income tax?
items.rule_line: A high-income taxpayer's state and local tax cap is reduced by 30% of modified AGI over the threshold, so an action that lowers modified AGI gives a second deduction benefit.

why.A: Counts only the extra state and local tax deduction ($6,000 x 35%). The $20,000 deferral also reduces taxable income directly.
why.B: Counts only the salary deferral. It misses the larger state and local tax deduction that results from a lower modified AGI.
why.C: The deferral saves $20,000 x 35% = $7,000 directly. It also lowers modified AGI to $545,000, so the state and local tax cap rises from $22,400 to $28,400 and the deduction rises by $6,000, saving another $2,100. Total $9,100.
why.D: Assumes the SALT deduction rises by the full $20,000 of deferral. The cap rises by only 30% of the reduction in modified AGI, or $6,000.

items.law_note: Cap amount, threshold, 30% reduction and $10,000 floor are stem assumptions based on P.L. 119-21 §70120 (cap $40,000 for 2025, 1% higher for 2026; threshold $500,000 for 2025, 1% higher for 2026). Confirmed 26 USC 164(b)(7): $40,000 (2025), $40,400 (2026); threshold $500,000 / $505,000; reduction 30% of MAGI excess; floor $10,000.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Itemized vs standard deduction / Analysis

guide.ask: What does the deferral save directly?
How does it change the state and local tax cap?
guide.reveal: Modified AGI falls to $545,000, so the cap rises from $22,400 to $28,400, a $6,000 larger deduction, worth $2,100. Total $9,100.

items.area_name: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
items.group_name: Individual compliance and tax planning for gross income, AGI, taxable income and estimated taxes
items.task: Consider the effect of changing tax rates and legislation on the timing of income and expense items for planning purposes given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Tomas Ruiz, single, has realized $30,000 of long-term capital gain in 2026 and has no other capital transactions. On December 10 he holds Stock X, bought seven months earlier, with a $15,000 unrealized loss. Assume net long-term capital gain is taxed at 15%, ordinary income at 32%, and the net investment income tax does not apply. He considers three plans. Plan 1: sell Stock X on December 10 and buy the same shares back on December 20. Plan 2: sell Stock X on December 10 and buy the same shares back on January 15, 2027. Plan 3: keep Stock X. Which plan gives the largest 2026 federal tax reduction, and by how much?
options: Plan 1, because the loss is realized in 2026 and reduces tax by $2,250
Plan 2, because the short-term loss is deducted at 32% and reduces tax by $4,800
Plans 1 and 2 give the same $2,250 reduction, because the repurchase date does not affect the loss
Plan 2, because the loss is realized in 2026 and reduces tax by $2,250
items.rule_line: A loss on a sale of stock is disallowed if substantially identical stock is bought within 30 days before or after the sale; an allowed short-term loss first offsets long-term gain in the netting.

why.A: Buying the same shares back within 30 days after the sale is a wash sale, so the $15,000 loss is disallowed and added to the basis of the new shares. Plan 1 gives no 2026 reduction.
why.B: The short-term loss is first netted against long-term gain, so it saves tax at the 15% long-term rate. It is not deducted at the ordinary rate because it is absorbed by gain.
why.C: The repurchase date decides the result. A repurchase within 30 days before or after the sale makes it a wash sale and defers the loss.
why.D: January 15 is 36 days after the sale, outside the 30-day wash sale period, so the loss counts in 2026. The $15,000 short-term loss nets against the $30,000 long-term gain, leaving $15,000 of long-term gain: tax falls from $4,500 to $2,250, a reduction of $2,250.

steps: Wash sale window: December 10 plus 30 days ends January 9, so January 15 is outside it (36 days)
Reduction = 4,500 - 2,250 = 2,250; Plan 1 loss is disallowed, so no reduction
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 1091(a): 30 days before and after the sale date.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Timing planning / Analysis

guide.ask: How long is the wash sale window after a sale, and where do the repurchase dates fall?
guide.reveal: Thirty days after the sale ends January 9, so a repurchase on December 20 is inside and one on January 15 is outside.

guide.ask: If the loss counts, how does it net against the gain?
guide.reveal: The short-term loss of $15,000 offsets long-term gain, leaving $15,000 taxed at 15%: $2,250 instead of $4,500.

guide.ask: Compare the plans.
guide.reveal: Only the plan whose repurchase falls outside the window gets the $2,250 reduction.

items.area_name: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
items.group_name: Individual compliance and tax planning for gross income, AGI, taxable income and estimated taxes
items.task: Consider the effect of changing tax rates and legislation on the timing of income and expense items for planning purposes given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Wendy Park, single, is a sole proprietor with 2026 net profit of $180,000 from a business that is not a specified service business. Her taxable income is below the level at which the wage and property limits apply, so her qualified business income deduction equals 20% of qualified business income, and the taxable income limit does not restrict it. Qualified business income is reduced by any deductible retirement plan contribution. Assume her marginal rate is 24% throughout and all of a $30,000 SEP-IRA contribution is deductible. By how much does the SEP-IRA contribution reduce her 2026 federal income tax?
items.rule_line: A deductible retirement contribution by a self-employed owner reduces qualified business income, so the net taxable income reduction is 80% of the contribution.

why.A: Computes only the effect of the lower qualified business income deduction ($6,000 x 24%). The contribution itself is also deducted.
why.B: The contribution lowers AGI and taxable income by $30,000 but also lowers qualified business income by $30,000, which cuts the 20% deduction by $6,000. Taxable income falls by a net $24,000, so tax falls by $24,000 x 24% = $5,760.
why.C: This is the amount of qualified business income deduction lost, $6,000, not a tax amount. The reduction is measured in tax, at her rate.
why.D: Ignores that the deductible contribution also reduces qualified business income and the 20% deduction. Tax falls by less than $30,000 x 24%.

steps: Contribution reduces AGI and taxable income by 30,000
Qualified business income falls 30,000, so the deduction falls 20% x 30,000 = 6,000
Net taxable income reduction = 30,000 - 6,000 = 24,000; tax reduction = 24,000 x 24% = 5,760
items.law_note: The 20% qualified business income deduction is permanent for tax years after 2025 under P.L. 119-21 §70105, so 2026 use depends on that Act. Confirmed 26 USC 199A(i) as amended: deduction permanent after 2025.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Timing planning / Analysis

guide.ask: What does the SEP contribution do to taxable income directly?
guide.reveal: It lowers AGI and taxable income by $30,000.

guide.ask: What is the side effect on the 20% deduction?
guide.reveal: Qualified business income falls by $30,000, so the deduction falls by $6,000; net taxable income drop is $24,000, saving 24% x $24,000 = $5,760.

items.task: Identify projected tax savings through utilization of flexible spending accounts (FSAs) and qualified health savings accounts (HSAs) for planning purposes given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Marta Keller, age 40, is single with a child and has family coverage under a qualifying high-deductible health plan, so her 2026 HSA limit is $8,750. She expects $6,000 of qualified medical expenses in 2026. Her AGI before any HSA contribution is $80,000 and she is in the 22% bracket. Her other itemizable deductions total $9,000, well below the $16,100 standard deduction. She can (1) pay the $6,000 with after-tax dollars, or (2) contribute $6,000 to an HSA through her employer's cafeteria plan by salary reduction and pay the expenses from the HSA. Assume employee FICA is 7.65% on her wages, she is below the Social Security wage base, and medical expenses are deductible only above 7.5% of AGI. How much lower is her combined 2026 federal income tax and employee FICA under choice (2) than under choice (1)?
items.rule_line: A medical expense paid through a pre-tax HSA salary reduction saves income tax and FICA, while the itemized deduction gives nothing if it falls below the 7.5% floor or the standard deduction.

why.A: Counts only FICA. The salary reduction also removes the $6,000 from taxable income and saves income tax at 22%.
why.B: Counts only income tax. Contributions made by salary reduction through a cafeteria plan also avoid employee FICA.
why.C: Under choice (1) no itemized medical deduction arises: the 7.5% floor is $6,000, and her itemized total is below the standard deduction anyway. Under choice (2) the salary reduction avoids both income tax (22%) and FICA (7.65%): $6,000 x 29.65% = $1,779.
why.D: Uses 15.3%, which is the combined employer and employee FICA rate. Only the employee's 7.65% is her cost.

steps: Choice 1: 7.5% x 80,000 = 6,000 floor, so the medical deduction is 0; itemized 9,000 < 16,100, so no tax benefit
Choice 2: salary reduction of 6,000 avoids income tax 6,000 x 22% = 1,320 and FICA 6,000 x 7.65% = 459
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / FSA/HSA / Analysis

guide.ask: Does she get any medical deduction paying with after-tax dollars?
guide.reveal: No: the 7.5% floor is $6,000 and her itemized total is below the standard deduction anyway.

guide.ask: What does salary reduction into the HSA avoid?

items.area_name: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
items.group_name: Individual compliance and tax planning for gross income, AGI, taxable income and estimated taxes
items.task: Consider the impact of using either itemized deductions or the standard deduction for planning purposes given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Ed Rossi, age 74, single, must take a $30,000 required minimum distribution from his traditional IRA in 2026 and wants to give $10,000 to his church. He has a $165,000 pension, and $12,000 of other itemizable deductions. Assume his standard deduction is $18,150, his income is high enough that any extra deduction for taxpayers age 65 or older is fully phased out, and he is in the 24% bracket at all the relevant income levels. Assume that charitable gifts of cash are deductible only above 0.5% of AGI. Option 1: take the full $30,000 distribution and give $10,000 of cash to the church. Option 2: direct the IRA custodian to send $10,000 to the church as a qualified charitable distribution and take the other $20,000 as his required distribution. Ed uses the larger of itemized and standard deductions each way. How much lower is his 2026 federal income tax under Option 2?
items.rule_line: A qualified charitable distribution is excluded from gross income and counts toward the required distribution, and it beats a cash gift because the cash gift is subject to the AGI floor and to the choice of standard deduction.

why.A: Deducts the full $10,000 gift in Option 1 and ignores the 0.5% of AGI floor. The floor removes $975 of the gift deduction.
why.B: Option 1: AGI is $195,000, the gift is deductible only above the $975 floor, so itemized deductions are $12,000 + $9,025 = $21,025, above the standard deduction. Option 2: AGI is $185,000 and itemized deductions of $12,000 are below the standard deduction, so he takes $18,150. Taxable income is $173,975 versus $166,850, a difference of $7,125, and tax is $1,710 lower.
why.C: Assumes the gift saves nothing under Option 1 and the exclusion saves the full $10,000 at 24%. In Option 1 he itemizes and gets a deduction for most of the gift.
why.D: Applies the rate to the $20,000 of distribution he still takes. The QCD keeps only the $10,000 given to the church out of income.

steps: Option 2: AGI = 165,000 + 20,000 = 185,000; itemized 12,000 < 18,150, so standard deduction; taxable income = 185,000 - 18,150 = 166,850
items.law_note: The 0.5% AGI floor on itemized charitable gifts starts in 2026 (P.L. 119-21 §70425); the stem states it. The senior deduction phase-out is stated in the stem. Confirmed 26 USC 170(b)(1)(I) 0.5% of contribution base floor. The 65-and-older extra deduction is assumed phased out in the stem.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Itemized vs standard deduction / Analysis

guide.ask: What is his AGI and itemized total when he gives cash?
guide.reveal: AGI $195,000; the gift is deductible above $975, so $9,025; itemized $12,000 + $9,025 = $21,025.

guide.ask: What happens when the gift is a direct transfer from the IRA?
guide.reveal: AGI falls to $185,000 and the $12,000 itemized total is below the $18,150 standard deduction, so taxable income is $166,850 versus $173,975.

guide.ask: Compute the tax difference.

items.area_name: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
items.group_name: Compliance for passive activity and at-risk loss limitations (excluding tax credit implications)
items.task: Calculate the passive activity loss limitations given a specific scenario, including the netting of passive activity gains and losses.
items.stem: Jonah Reyes and his wife file jointly and have $400,000 of modified AGI, so the special $25,000 allowance for rental losses is not available. Jonah owns three rental buildings that produce a combined 2026 loss of $60,000, and he is in the 37% bracket. He has a valid election to treat all his rental real estate interests as one activity. His wife does no rental work. Jonah works as an engineer for an unrelated employer for 1,500 hours a year, and spends 900 hours a year on his rentals. He can cut his engineering hours without changing his rental hours. Which choice makes the rental loss deductible against his other income for 2026, and what is the tax saving?
options: Reduce the engineering work to 900 hours, since rental hours would then equal the engineering hours, and save $22,200
Make no change, because 900 rental hours exceeds 750 hours and already meets the test, saving $22,200
No reduction of engineering hours can make the loss deductible, because employee wages prevent real estate professional status, so the saving is $0
Reduce the engineering work to 800 hours, which meets both hour tests, and save $22,200
items.rule_line: A taxpayer is a real estate professional only if more than half of personal service hours, and more than 750 hours, are in real property trades in which he materially participates; then rental losses are not passive.

why.A: Equal hours (900 of 1,800, or 50%) is not more than half. The test requires more than 50% of personal service hours in real estate trades.
why.B: The 750-hour test is only one of two tests. At 1,500 engineering hours, 900 / 2,400 = 37.5%, so the more-than-half test fails and the loss stays passive.
why.C: Wage work does not bar real estate professional status. The wage hours count only in the more-than-half test, and cutting them makes the test pass.
why.D: Real estate professional status needs more than 750 hours in real estate trades and more than half of all personal service hours in them. With 800 engineering hours, 900 / 1,700 = 52.9%. The election to combine the rentals gives him 900 hours in one activity, so he materially participates and the loss is not passive: $60,000 x 37% = $22,200.

steps: Test 1: 900 hours > 750 hours (passes at any engineering level)
Test 2 at 1,500 engineering hours: 900 / (900 + 1,500) = 37.5%, fails
At 900 engineering hours: 900 / 1,800 = 50%, not more than half, fails
At 800 engineering hours: 900 / 1,700 = 52.9%, passes; loss becomes nonpassive: 60,000 x 37% = 22,200
items.law_note: Employee work counts as personal services in a trade or business; only services as an employee of a company in which the employee owns more than 5% are treated as real property trade services. Confirmed Reg. 1.469-9(c)(5) (employee services count as trade or business services but not real property services unless 5% owner, so they enter only the denominator) and (g) (aggregation election).
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group B / Passive activity loss / Analysis

guide.ask: What two hour tests must a real estate professional pass?
guide.reveal: More than 750 hours in real property trades, and more than half of all personal service hours in them.

guide.ask: Which test does Jonah pass now, and which does he fail?
guide.reveal: 900 hours passes the first; at 1,500 engineering hours his share is 900 / 2,400 = 37.5%, which fails.

guide.ask: What engineering level gives a share above half with 900 rental hours, and what does the combining election add?
guide.reveal: Fewer than 900 engineering hours, so the second test passes and material participation follows: the loss is nonpassive and saves $60,000 x 37% = $22,200.

items.area_name: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
items.group_name: Compliance for passive activity and at-risk loss limitations (excluding tax credit implications)
items.task: Calculate the at-risk loss limitation for an activity in which an individual materially participates, including losses from pass-through entities and losses from real estate rental activities with active participation.
items.stem: Kira Sato is a limited partner in a partnership that is a passive activity to her. Her share of the partnership's 2026 loss is $90,000. Her basis in the partnership interest at year-end is $70,000 and her at-risk amount is $50,000. She also has $35,000 of net income from another passive activity. She considers contributing $30,000 in cash to the partnership before December 31, which would raise both her basis and her at-risk amount by $30,000. By how much would the contribution increase her deductible 2026 loss from the partnership?
items.rule_line: A loss is limited first by basis, then by the amount at risk, then by the passive activity rules, so extra basis or at-risk amount does not help when the passive limit is binding.

why.A: The loss must pass three limits in order: basis, at-risk, then passive. Without the contribution, the at-risk limit allows $50,000 but only $35,000 of passive income can absorb it. With the contribution, the at-risk limit rises to $80,000 but the passive limit still allows only $35,000. The deductible loss is $35,000 either way, an increase of $0.
why.B: Applies only the basis limit, which rises from $70,000 to $90,000 (the loss). The at-risk and passive activity limits are more restrictive.
why.C: Applies only the at-risk limit, which rises by $30,000. The passive activity limit caps the loss at $35,000 in both cases.
why.D: Subtracts the passive income from the new at-risk limit. This is the loss that is still suspended after the contribution, not the increase in the deduction.

steps: Without contribution: min(90,000 loss, 70,000 basis, 50,000 at risk) = 50,000; passive limit 35,000; deductible = 35,000
With contribution: min(90,000, 100,000, 80,000) = 80,000; passive limit 35,000; deductible = 35,000
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group B / At-risk limitation / Analysis

guide.ask: In what order do basis, at-risk and passive limits apply?
guide.reveal: Basis first, then at-risk, then the passive rules.

guide.ask: What does the passive limit allow here regardless of the contribution?
guide.reveal: Her $35,000 of other passive income, so the at-risk limit of $50,000 is not the binding one.

guide.ask: Increase from the contribution?
guide.reveal: Deductible is $35,000 both ways, so $0.

items.area_name: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
items.task: Identify the potential tax savings from gifting ownership of noncash property to an individual given a specific planning scenario, including identification of the property to be gifted to minimize the donor's future estate.
items.stem: Ines Varga, age 78, wants to give her son $200,000 of securities now. She owns Stock A (worth $200,000, basis $40,000) and Stock B (worth $200,000, basis $260,000), both held long term. She will keep whichever stock she does not give until death, and her estate is well below the estate tax exemption. Her son will sell whatever he receives right away. Long-term capital gain is taxed at 15% for both, and Ines has large capital gains this year, so any loss she realizes saves tax at 15%. Plan 1: give Stock A. Plan 2: give Stock B. Plan 3: sell Stock B, and give the $200,000 of cash. Which plan gives the lowest combined income tax for Ines and her son?
options: Plan 1, with combined tax of $24,000
Plan 2, because the son sells with no gain or loss and Ines keeps Stock A for a stepped-up basis
Plans 2 and 3 equally, each with combined tax of $0
Plan 3, which produces a net tax saving of $9,000
items.rule_line: A gift of appreciated property carries over the donor's basis, and a gift of loss property gives the donee no loss deduction; a donor with loss property should sell it and give the cash, and keep appreciated property for a step-up at death.

why.A: The son takes Stock A with Ines's $40,000 basis and taxes $160,000 of gain at 15%, which is $24,000. Ines also loses the step-up on Stock A.
why.B: Combined tax is $0, but the loss is wasted: for a loss the son's basis is the $200,000 value, so his sale shows no loss, and Ines's $60,000 loss disappears at her death.
why.C: Plan 3 produces a $9,000 saving while Plan 2 produces none. A gift of loss property gives up the loss for both the donor and the donee.
why.D: Ines sells Stock B and uses the $60,000 loss against gains, saving $60,000 x 15% = $9,000. The cash gift carries no income tax for the son, and Stock A, held until death, gets a step-up. Combined tax is negative $9,000.

steps: Plan 1: son's gain = 200,000 - 40,000 = 160,000; tax = 160,000 x 15% = 24,000; B basis steps down at death
Plan 2: loss basis = 200,000 (value), so son sells at 200,000 with no gain or loss; tax 0, and the 60,000 loss is never used
Plan 3: loss = 260,000 - 200,000 = 60,000; saving = 60,000 x 15% = 9,000; Stock A keeps its step-up
Lowest combined tax is Plan 3 (net saving of 9,000)
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group C / Gifting for planning / Analysis

guide.ask: What happens if she gives the appreciated stock, and if she gives the loss stock?
guide.reveal: The son takes her basis: gain of $160,000 for the first ($24,000 tax); for the loss stock the son's loss basis falls to value, so no loss is ever used.

guide.ask: What does selling the loss stock first produce, and what happens to the stock she keeps?
guide.reveal: A $60,000 loss that saves $9,000, and the appreciated stock keeps its step-up at death.

guide.ask: Lowest combined tax?
guide.reveal: The sell-first plan, a net saving of $9,000.

items.area_name: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
items.task: Calculate the amount of taxable gifts for federal gift tax purposes.
items.stem: In 2026 Hal and Eve Dorn, who are married and consent to split all gifts, make these transfers. Hal gives $200,000 to a 529 plan for his granddaughter Ada and elects to spread the gift over five years. Eve gives $15,000 in cash to their grandson Ben. Hal also pays $12,000 of tuition directly to Ben's university. Assume the annual exclusion is $19,000 per donee and ignore the lifetime exemption. What total amount of taxable gifts do Hal and Eve report on their two gift tax returns for 2026?
items.rule_line: Gift splitting treats each spouse as making half of every gift, and a 529 five-year election lets each donor apply five annual exclusions to a large contribution; direct tuition payments are excluded.

why.A: Assumes the five-year election covers the whole $200,000. Two spouses can apply five exclusions each, $190,000 in total, so $10,000 is taxable.
why.B: Counts the taxable excess for only one spouse. Each spouse is treated as making half of the gift, so both returns show a taxable amount.
why.C: With splitting, each spouse is treated as giving half: $100,000 to Ada and $7,500 to Ben. The five-year election lets each spouse use five annual exclusions ($95,000) on the 529 gift, leaving $5,000 taxable each, or $10,000. Ben's $7,500 share each is under the $19,000 exclusion, and the direct tuition payment is excluded.
why.D: Ignores gift splitting and reports the whole $105,000 excess on Hal's return. With splitting, the $200,000 gift uses two donors' five-year exclusions.

steps: Splitting: each spouse gives half: Ada 100,000 each, Ben 7,500 each
Five-year election: each spouse excludes 5 x 19,000 = 95,000 for Ada; taxable = 100,000 - 95,000 = 5,000 each = 10,000
Ben: 7,500 < 19,000 exclusion each, taxable 0; tuition of 12,000 paid directly is excluded
Total taxable gifts = 10,000
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 529(c)(2)(B) five-year election.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group C / Taxable gifts / Analysis

guide.ask: How does gift splitting change the amounts?
guide.reveal: Each spouse gives half: $100,000 to Ada and $7,500 to Ben.

guide.ask: How does the five-year election apply, and what about the tuition?
guide.reveal: Each spouse excludes 5 x $19,000 = $95,000 for Ada, leaving $5,000 taxable each; Ben's $7,500 is under the exclusion and direct tuition is excluded. Total taxable gifts are $10,000.

items.task: Identify the potential tax savings from gifting ownership of noncash property to an individual given a specific planning scenario, including identification of the property to be gifted to minimize the donor's future estate.
items.stem: Gwen Alvarez owns a rental building worth $400,000 with an adjusted basis of $100,000, subject to a $150,000 mortgage. Plan A: she gives the building to her son, who assumes the mortgage. Plan B: she uses $150,000 of her own cash to pay off the mortgage and then gives the building to her son free and clear. In either plan the son sells the building immediately for $400,000 (and repays any mortgage). Ignore gift tax rates, depreciation recapture, and the annual exclusion. Compare Plan A with Plan B. Which statement is correct?
options: Plan A produces less combined gain, $250,000, and the gift is $250,000 instead of $400,000
Plan A produces more combined gain, $350,000, and the gift is $250,000 instead of $400,000
Plan A produces the same $300,000 of combined gain as Plan B, and the gift is $250,000 instead of $400,000
Plan A produces the same $300,000 of combined gain as Plan B, and the gift is $400,000 in both plans
items.rule_line: When property subject to debt is given and the donee assumes the debt, the transfer is part sale and part gift: the donor's gain is the debt relief less basis, the gift is the value less the debt, and the donee's basis is the greater of the amount paid or the donor's basis.

why.A: This counts only the son's gain in Plan A. Gwen also recognizes $50,000 of gain on the part of the transfer that is a sale.
why.B: Adds Gwen's $50,000 gain to the son's gain measured from her $100,000 basis ($300,000). The son's basis is raised to $150,000, the amount paid, which removes the overlap.
why.C: In Plan A the transfer is part gift, part sale. Gwen's gain is $150,000 debt relief less her $100,000 basis, or $50,000. The son's basis is the greater of the debt assumed or her basis, $150,000, so his gain is $250,000. Combined gain is $300,000, the same as Plan B (son's gain of $400,000 - $100,000). The gift is $400,000 - $150,000 = $250,000 in Plan A, against $400,000 in Plan B.
why.D: The debt the son assumes is consideration for the transfer, so the gift is only the value above that. In Plan B, Gwen pays off her own mortgage and the whole $400,000 is a gift.

steps: Plan B: no gain to Gwen; son's basis = 100,000; son's gain = 300,000; gift = 400,000
Combined gain is 300,000 in both plans; the gift differs
items.law_note: Confirmed Reg. 1.1015-4 (greater of amount paid or donor's basis) and Reg. 1.1001-1(e)(1) (gain = amount realized less adjusted basis, no loss).

items.stem: Cal and Dee Ito, who file jointly, expect 2026 modified AGI of $215,000, which includes $70,000 of net investment income. They are considering converting $80,000 from a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA and paying the tax from other funds. Assume the conversion income is taxed at a flat 24% and the net investment income tax rate is 3.8% with a $250,000 threshold for joint filers. How much additional federal tax, including any net investment income tax, does the conversion cause for 2026?
items.rule_line: The net investment income tax applies to the lesser of net investment income or modified AGI above the threshold, and a Roth conversion increases modified AGI even though it is not investment income.

why.A: This is only the net investment income tax the conversion triggers ($1,710). The conversion income is also taxed at 24%.
why.B: Applies the 3.8% tax to the conversion itself and leaves out the income tax. A Roth conversion is ordinary income, and it is not net investment income; it only raises modified AGI.
why.C: Counts only the income tax on the conversion and misses the net investment income tax it triggers by raising modified AGI over the threshold.
why.D: The conversion is ordinary income of $80,000 taxed at 24% ($19,200). It is not investment income, but it raises modified AGI to $295,000, which is $45,000 over the threshold. The 3.8% tax applies to the lesser of net investment income ($70,000) or the excess ($45,000), or $1,710. Total $20,910.

steps: Conversion income tax = 80,000 x 24% = 19,200
Modified AGI after conversion = 215,000 + 80,000 = 295,000; excess over 250,000 = 45,000
Net investment income tax = 3.8% x min(70,000, 45,000) = 1,710 (before conversion the excess was 0)

items.stem: Pete Novak, age 60, separated from service in 2026. His 401(k) account holds only employer stock with a cost basis of $100,000 and a value of $400,000, and he takes a lump-sum distribution of the entire account in 2026. Option A: take the stock in kind, pay tax on the $100,000 basis now, and sell the stock 18 months later for $450,000. Option B: roll the account to a traditional IRA and later withdraw $450,000 in one year, after the stock has grown to that value. Assume his ordinary rate is 24% and his long-term capital gain rate is 15% in all years, the 10% early distribution tax does not apply, and ignore the time value of money. How much less total federal income tax does Option A produce than Option B?
items.rule_line: On a lump-sum distribution of employer stock, tax on the net unrealized appreciation is deferred to the sale and taxed as long-term gain, while the cost basis is ordinary income at distribution; a rollover to an IRA taxes everything as ordinary income.

why.A: Gives Option A the favorable rate only on the $50,000 of appreciation after distribution ($50,000 x 9%). The $300,000 of net unrealized appreciation gets long-term capital gain treatment.
why.B: Option A: $100,000 basis is ordinary income now ($24,000). The $300,000 of net unrealized appreciation is long-term gain when sold, and so is the $50,000 of later growth because he held the shares more than a year after distribution ($350,000 x 15% = $52,500). Total $76,500. Option B taxes $450,000 as ordinary income at 24% ($108,000). Difference $31,500.
why.C: Applies the capital gain rate to the whole $450,000. The $100,000 basis is taxed as ordinary income when distributed.
why.D: This is the total tax under Option A ($76,500), not the savings compared with Option B.

steps: Net unrealized appreciation = 400,000 - 100,000 = 300,000; growth after distribution = 450,000 - 400,000 = 50,000
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 402(e)(4)(B), (D): lump sum within one taxable year after a triggering event (age 59 1/2 or separation).

items.stem: Sylvia Tran, single, age 62, needs $100,000 of cash in 2026 and has no other income. She can raise it from her traditional IRA, from a taxable brokerage account of long-term holdings whose basis is 10% of their value, or from both. Plan 1: withdraw $100,000 from the IRA. Plan 2: sell $100,000 of brokerage holdings. Plan 3: withdraw $50,000 from the IRA and sell $50,000 of brokerage holdings. Assume a $16,100 standard deduction, ordinary rates of 10% on taxable income up to $12,400, 12% up to $50,400 and 22% up to $105,700, and long-term capital gain rates of 0% on taxable income up to $49,450 and 15% above that, with capital gain stacked on top of ordinary taxable income. Ignore the net investment income tax and state taxes. Which plan has the lowest 2026 federal income tax?
options: Plan 1, with tax of about $13,170
Plan 3, with tax of about $8,238
Plans 2 and 3 equally, because both use the 0% capital gain rate on part of the gain
Plan 2, with tax of about $3,668
items.rule_line: Long-term capital gain is taxed at 0% only to the extent it fits in the low bracket after ordinary income, and the standard deduction can offset gain, so a withdrawal order that adds ordinary income can cost more than selling appreciated assets.

why.A: Withdrawing all $100,000 from the IRA makes it all ordinary income taxed up to the 22% bracket, the highest tax of the three plans.
why.B: The $50,000 IRA withdrawal uses up the standard deduction against ordinary income and pushes the gain into the 15% range, so the tax is higher than selling the brokerage holdings alone.
why.C: Both plans use some 0% bracket, but Plan 3 has ordinary income that occupies part of it and more gain above it, so the two taxes differ.
why.D: The sale produces $90,000 of long-term gain and no ordinary income. The standard deduction reduces the gain to $73,900 of taxable income, of which $49,450 is at 0% and $24,450 at 15%: about $3,668.

steps: Plan 3: ordinary taxable income = 50,000 - 16,100 = 33,900, tax 3,820; gain 45,000 stacked above it, 15,550 at 0% and 29,450 at 15% = 4,418; total 8,238
Plan 2 has the lowest tax

items.task: Calculate the tax realized and recognized gain (loss) for both a C corporation and shareholders on a nonliquidating distribution of noncash property, and the shareholders' basis in the property received.
items.stem: Harbor Tool Corp., a C corporation with ample earnings and profits taxed at a flat 21%, will transfer $250,000 of value to its sole shareholder. It owns Asset X, worth $150,000 with an adjusted basis of $50,000, and Asset Y, worth $100,000 with an adjusted basis of $160,000. Both are business assets held more than a year, and any net gain or loss is taxed or deducted at 21%. Plan 1: distribute both assets in kind. Plan 2: sell Asset Y to an unrelated buyer for $100,000 in cash, then distribute Asset X and the $100,000 of cash. The shareholder receives a $250,000 dividend either way. How much less total corporate income tax does Plan 2 produce than Plan 1?
items.rule_line: A corporation recognizes gain, but not loss, when it distributes property to shareholders, so loss property should be sold before the distribution and the cash distributed.

why.A: This is the corporate tax under Plan 2, not the difference between the plans.
why.B: Plan 1: the corporation recognizes the $100,000 gain on Asset X and cannot deduct the $60,000 loss on Asset Y, so tax is $21,000. Plan 2: the loss on the sale of Y is recognized and offsets the gain on X, so tax is 21% x $40,000 = $8,400. The difference is $12,600.
why.C: This is the corporate tax under Plan 1, not the savings from Plan 2.
why.D: Multiplies the basis of Asset Y by 21%. The loss that is recovered in Plan 2 is the $60,000 of built-in loss, not the whole basis.

guide.reveal: No, a loss on a distribution of property is not recognized.

guide.ask: What is the tax under the distribute-both plan?
guide.reveal: Gain of $100,000 on X is taxed: $21,000.

guide.reveal: The $60,000 loss offsets the gain: 21% x $40,000 = $8,400. Difference $12,600.

items.task: Recall the limitations on the use of net operating losses when there is an ownership change.
items.stem: Cobalt Ridge Corp. has an $800,000 net operating loss carryforward arising after 2017 and expects $600,000 of taxable income before any net operating loss deduction in 2027. Its stock is worth $2,000,000, and assume the long-term tax-exempt rate is 3.5%. An investor may buy stock in one of two ways. Plan A: buy 55% of the stock from existing shareholders in 2026. Plan B: buy 45% of the stock in 2026. Assume no other ownership shifts in the testing period, a 21% corporate rate, and that the net operating loss deduction is limited to 80% of taxable income before the deduction. How much more tax does Cobalt Ridge save in 2027 under Plan B than under Plan A?
items.rule_line: An ownership change of more than 50 percentage points limits the annual net operating loss use to the value of the loss corporation times the long-term tax-exempt rate; without a change, only the 80% of taxable income limit applies.

why.A: This is the saving under Plan A alone ($14,700), not the difference between the plans.
why.B: Subtracts the $70,000 limit itself instead of the tax it saves ($14,700). The comparison should be of tax savings under the two plans.
why.C: This is the annual limit under Plan A, $70,000, which is a deduction amount and not a tax saving.
why.D: Plan A: a 55-point shift is an ownership change, so the annual limit is $2,000,000 x 3.5% = $70,000 and the deduction is $70,000 (saving $14,700). Plan B: 45 points is not more than 50, so there is no ownership change and the 80% limit allows $480,000 (saving $100,800). Difference $86,100.

steps: Plan B: no ownership change (45 points); deduction = min(800,000, 80% x 600,000 = 480,000) = 480,000; saving = 480,000 x 21% = 100,800
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 382(b)(1) (value x long-term tax-exempt rate) and 382(g)(1) (more than 50 percentage points).

guide.ask: What is the deduction if there is a change?
What if there is no change?

items.task: Calculate the tax realized and recognized gain (loss) for both a C corporation and shareholders on a nonliquidating distribution of noncash property, and the shareholders' basis in the property received.
items.stem: Basil Corp., a C corporation with ample earnings and profits taxed at 21%, owns an investment asset held for two years. The asset has an adjusted basis of $200,000 and is worth $120,000. Basil Corp. has enough capital gains this year to absorb any capital loss on the asset. Its sole shareholder wants $120,000 of value out of the corporation. Plan 1: the corporation sells the asset to the shareholder for $120,000. Plan 2: the corporation distributes the asset to the shareholder. Plan 3: the corporation sells the asset to an unrelated buyer for $120,000 and distributes the cash. In which plan or plans does the corporation deduct the $80,000 loss, and what is the corporate tax saving?
options: Plan 3 only, because the other plans are a related party sale and a distribution, so it saves $16,800
Plan 1 only, because a sale to the sole shareholder at value is a completed exchange, saving $16,800
Plans 1 and 2, because the asset leaves the corporation at a value below its basis, saving $16,800
Plans 2 and 3, because a distribution is treated as a sale at value, and each saves $16,800
items.rule_line: A corporation cannot deduct a loss on a distribution of property or on a sale to a more-than-50% shareholder; a sale to an unrelated buyer produces a deductible loss.

why.A: Plan 1 is a sale to a more-than-50% shareholder, so the loss is disallowed. Plan 2 is a distribution, so no loss is recognized. Only the sale to an unrelated buyer gives a deductible $80,000 loss, saving $80,000 x 21% = $16,800.
why.B: A loss on a sale between a corporation and a shareholder who owns more than 50% of its stock is disallowed, even if the sale is at value.
why.C: Neither plan allows the loss. The sale to the controlling shareholder is disallowed as a related party sale, and a loss on a distribution is never recognized.
why.D: A distribution is treated as a sale at value only for gain, not for loss, so Plan 2 gives no deduction.

steps: Plan 1: related party sale (sole shareholder owns 100%), loss of 80,000 disallowed
Plan 2: distribution of loss property, loss not recognized
Plan 3: sale to an unrelated buyer, loss = 200,000 - 120,000 = 80,000, tax saving = 80,000 x 21% = 16,800
Only Plan 3 gives a deductible loss
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 267(a)(1), (b)(2) (more than 50% in value).

guide.ask: When is a loss disallowed under the related-party rules and when is it not recognized at all?
guide.reveal: A sale to a more-than-50% owner is disallowed; a distribution of loss property is not recognized.

guide.ask: Which path gives a deductible loss?
guide.reveal: Only the sale to an unrelated buyer: $200,000 - $120,000 = $80,000, saving 21% x $80,000 = $16,800.

items.task: Calculate the amount and treatment of the cash distributions to shareholders in excess of a C corporation's current and accumulated earnings and profits (E&P).
items.stem: Ray Ostrom owns 60% of the stock of Ostrom Co., a C corporation with ample earnings and profits. His son Sam owns the other 40%. Ray's basis in his shares is $100,000 and he can get $500,000 for them. Plan 1: the corporation redeems all of Ray's shares and no agreement is filed. Plan 2: the corporation redeems all of Ray's shares, and Ray files the required agreement, will hold no interest in the corporation other than as a creditor (not as an officer, director, or employee) for 10 years, and has not transferred stock to Sam or received stock from Sam in the previous 10 years. Plan 3: Ray sells all of his shares to Sam for $500,000. Assume qualified dividends and long-term capital gain are both taxed at 20%. What is Ray's federal income tax on each plan?
items.rule_line: A redemption of all of a shareholder's stock is a sale or exchange only if family attribution does not leave the shareholder with a constructive interest, which requires a waiver; otherwise the redemption is a dividend to the extent of earnings and profits.

why.A: In Plan 1 Ray is treated as owning Sam's shares, so after the redemption he still owns 100% and the payment is a $500,000 dividend ($100,000). In Plan 2 the waiver of attribution lets the redemption count as a complete termination and gives a $400,000 gain ($80,000). In Plan 3 the sale to Sam is a sale, with a $400,000 gain.
why.B: Ignores family attribution. Without the waiver, Ray is treated as owning his son's shares, so the redemption is not a complete termination and is a dividend.
why.C: The waiver in Plan 2 is what allows attribution from Sam to be ignored, so a complete termination redemption gives capital gain treatment.
why.D: A sale of stock to a related person is a sale, and gain is reported at capital gain rates. The dividend rule applies only to distributions by the corporation.

steps: Plan 1: constructive ownership of Sam's 40% means Ray still owns 100% after the redemption, so the $500,000 is a dividend: 500,000 x 20% = 100,000
Plan 2: with the waiver, complete termination gives exchange treatment: gain = 500,000 - 100,000 = 400,000; tax = 400,000 x 20% = 80,000
Plan 3: sale to Sam: gain 400,000, tax 80,000
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 302(c)(2) waiver conditions (no interest other than creditor, 10-year rule, agreement).

guide.ask: How does family attribution affect a redemption of Ray's shares with no agreement?
guide.reveal: Ray is treated as owning Sam's shares, so he still holds 100% and the payment is a dividend: 20% x $500,000 = $100,000.

guide.ask: What does a waiver of attribution do?
guide.reveal: It allows a complete termination, so exchange treatment: gain $500,000 - $100,000 = $400,000, tax $80,000.

guide.ask: What about a direct sale to Sam?
guide.reveal: A sale, with the same $400,000 gain and $80,000 tax.

items.task: Calculate the allocation of S corporation income (loss) after the sale of a shareholder's ownership interest in the S corporation for tax purposes.
items.stem: Ava Lund owns 50% of Kestrel, Inc., a calendar-year S corporation, with a stock basis of $100,000. On June 30, 2026 she sells all of her shares to an unrelated buyer for $500,000. Kestrel earned $400,000 of ordinary income in 2026, all of it in January through June. Ava's share of income can be figured on a per-day basis (181 of 365 days) or under the closing-of-the-books election at the sale date. Ava's rate is 37% on ordinary income and 20% on long-term capital gain. Ignore the net investment income tax. How much more total federal tax does Ava pay if the closing-of-the-books election is used rather than the per-day allocation, considering both her share of income and her gain on the sale?
items.rule_line: Income allocated to a selling S corporation shareholder increases stock basis and lowers the gain on the sale, so shifting income to the seller trades ordinary income for less capital gain.

why.A: Per-day: Ava reports $99,178 of income, raising her basis to $199,178 and leaving a $300,822 gain. Closing of the books: she reports all $200,000, basis $300,000, gain $200,000. The extra income of $100,822 is taxed at 37%, but it lowers the gain by the same amount, taxed at 20%. Net cost = $100,822 x 17% = $17,140.
why.B: Counts only the tax on the extra gain. The extra income is taxed at 37% and the gain falls by the same amount, so the net cost uses the difference between the two rates.
why.C: Counts only the tax on the extra ordinary income and ignores that it increases basis and lowers the gain on the sale.
why.D: This is the extra income allocated to Ava under the election, not a tax amount.

steps: Per-day income = 400,000 x 50% x 181/365 = 99,178; closing-of-the-books income = 200,000; extra = 100,822
Extra ordinary tax = 100,822 x 37% = 37,304; basis higher by 100,822, so gain lower by 100,822: 100,822 x 20% = 20,164 saved
items.law_note: Confirmed Reg. 1.1377-1(a)(2): the seller is treated as a shareholder for the day of the disposition, so a June 30 sale gives 181 days; (b)(5) requires consent of the corporation and each affected shareholder.

items.task: Calculate the impact on a shareholder's stock basis in an S corporation for tax purposes resulting from nonliquidating distributions of noncash property.
items.stem: Lior Mizrahi owns all of Fable Co., a calendar-year S corporation. His stock basis on January 1, 2026 is $70,000, and he has no debt basis. Fable expects a $60,000 ordinary loss for 2026 and no other items. Lior plans to take a $50,000 cash distribution. Plan 1: take it in November 2026. Plan 2: take it in January 2027. Ignore any effect on 2027. How much more of the 2026 loss can Lior deduct under Plan 2 than under Plan 1?
items.rule_line: An S corporation shareholder's stock basis is increased by income and contributions, decreased by distributions, and only then decreased by losses, so a distribution taken before year-end can cut off the deduction of a loss.

why.A: Assumes losses reduce basis before distributions, so timing would not matter. The ordering rule reduces basis by distributions first.
why.B: This is the basis left at the end of 2026 if the whole loss is deducted (Plan 2), not the additional loss that Plan 2 allows.
why.C: This is the loss Lior can deduct under Plan 1, not the difference between the plans.
why.D: Basis is reduced by distributions before it is reduced by losses. In Plan 1 the November distribution takes basis to $20,000, so only $20,000 of the loss is deductible and $40,000 is suspended. In Plan 2 basis is still $70,000 at year-end, so the full $60,000 is deductible. Difference $40,000.

steps: Plan 1: basis = 70,000 - 50,000 = 20,000 before losses; deductible loss = 20,000; suspended = 40,000
Plan 2: basis = 70,000 at year-end; deductible loss = 60,000
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 1367(a)(2): distributions reduce basis before losses.

guide.ask: Which reduces basis first, distributions or losses?
guide.reveal: Distributions first, in the same year.

guide.reveal: A November distribution leaves basis of $20,000 before the loss, so only $20,000 is deductible; a January distribution leaves $70,000, so the full $60,000 is deductible. Difference $40,000.

items.task: Calculate the impact on a shareholder's stock basis in an S corporation for tax purposes resulting from contributions of noncash property, including an S corporation's assumption of debt on the contributed property.
items.stem: Mona Lisle owns all of Zenith Corp., an S corporation that expects a $90,000 ordinary loss for 2026. Her stock basis at the start of the year is $10,000 and she has no debt basis. She wants to put $80,000 of value into Zenith before December 31. Plan 1: contribute long-term stock she owns, worth $80,000 with a basis of $30,000. Plan 2: sell the stock, pay 20% tax on the long-term capital gain, and contribute $80,000 of cash. She is in the 37% bracket and the loss is otherwise fully deductible. How much greater is her net 2026 tax benefit (tax saved on the deducted loss minus the capital gain tax) under Plan 2 than under Plan 1?
items.rule_line: Contributed property increases an S corporation shareholder's stock basis only by the property's adjusted basis, so selling appreciated property and contributing the cash can raise the basis at the price of a capital gain tax.

why.A: Plan 1: basis is $10,000 + $30,000 (basis of the contributed stock) = $40,000, so $40,000 of the loss is deducted (saving $14,800) and the gain is never taxed. Plan 2: basis is $90,000, so the full $90,000 is deducted (saving $33,300), less tax of $10,000 on the $50,000 gain, for $23,300. The difference is $8,500.
why.B: This is only the capital gain tax under Plan 2. The extra loss deduction it buys is worth more.
why.C: Counts the extra deduction of $50,000 at 37% but forgets the $10,000 of capital gain tax that Plan 2 costs.
why.D: This is the net benefit under Plan 2 alone ($23,300), not the excess over Plan 1.

items.law_note: Stock basis from a contribution comes from the general basis rules (26 USC 358/1012); 1367(a)(1) lists income items only. Cite corrected.

items.task: Calculate a partner's tax realized and recognized gain (loss) on the contribution of noncash property to a partnership, and the partnership's basis in the property contributed.
items.stem: Alpha contributes equipment with a tax basis of $40,000 and a value of $100,000 to a new partnership, and Beta contributes $100,000 of cash. The partners share all items equally. The equipment has a 10-year remaining life and is depreciated straight-line for both book and tax, so book depreciation is $10,000 a year and tax depreciation is $4,000 a year. Compare the traditional method with the remedial method for allocating the equipment's tax depreciation in the first year. Which statement is correct?
options: Under the remedial method Beta's taxable income is $1,000 lower and Alpha's is unchanged from the traditional method
Under the remedial method Beta's taxable income is unchanged and Alpha's is $1,000 higher than under the traditional method
Under the remedial method Beta's taxable income is $1,000 higher and Alpha's is $1,000 lower than under the traditional method
Under the remedial method Beta's taxable income is $1,000 lower and Alpha's is $1,000 higher than under the traditional method
items.rule_line: Under the traditional method the ceiling rule can leave the noncontributing partner with less tax depreciation than book depreciation, while the remedial method fixes the shortfall with an offsetting deduction to that partner and income to the contributing partner.

why.A: The remedial method creates an offsetting item for the contributing partner. Alpha reports $1,000 of remedial income, so Alpha's income is not unchanged.
why.B: Beta is the partner who benefits from the remedial deduction, so her income falls by $1,000. Both partners are affected.
why.C: Reverses the effect. The remedial method corrects Beta's shortfall of depreciation, so Beta gets the deduction and Alpha gets the income.
why.D: Beta's book share of depreciation is $5,000, but the ceiling rule limits tax depreciation to the $4,000 available, all of which goes to Beta under the traditional method. The remedial method gives Beta a $1,000 additional deduction and Alpha $1,000 of offsetting income.

steps: Book depreciation = 100,000 / 10 = 10,000; each partner's book share = 5,000; tax depreciation = 40,000 / 10 = 4,000
Traditional: Beta gets all 4,000 of tax depreciation (ceiling rule), a shortfall of 5,000 - 4,000 = 1,000; Alpha gets 0
Remedial: Beta gets an additional 1,000 deduction and Alpha reports 1,000 of remedial income
Beta's income is 1,000 lower and Alpha's is 1,000 higher under the remedial method
items.law_note: Confirmed Reg. 1.704-3(b)(1) ceiling rule and (d) remedial method (remedial deduction to the noncontributing partner, offsetting income to the contributor).
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group C / Contribution to partnership / Analysis

guide.ask: What is each partner's book share of depreciation, and what is the tax depreciation?
guide.reveal: Book $10,000 a year, $5,000 each; tax depreciation is $40,000 / 10 = $4,000.

guide.ask: What does the traditional method do with the $4,000?
guide.reveal: The ceiling rule gives all $4,000 to Beta, still $1,000 short of Beta's book share, and Alpha gets none.

guide.ask: What does the remedial method add?
guide.reveal: A $1,000 extra deduction for Beta and $1,000 of offsetting income for Alpha.

items.task: Calculate the impact on a partner's basis in a partnership for tax purposes resulting from nonliquidating distributions of noncash property.
items.stem: Cara Wolfe is a limited partner whose basis in her partnership interest is $50,000 at the start of 2026. Her share of 2026 partnership ordinary income is $10,000. During 2026 she receives a $40,000 cash distribution, and the partnership's repayment of a loan reduces her share of partnership liabilities by $35,000. Plan 1: make no contribution. Plan 2: contribute $20,000 in cash to the partnership on December 28, 2026. Plan 3: contribute $20,000 in cash on January 10, 2027. Which plan, or plans, avoid gain recognition for 2026?
options: Plans 2 and 3; a contribution before the return is filed restores basis, so there is no gain
Plan 2 only; Plans 1 and 3 each produce a $25,000 gain in 2026
Plan 2 only; Plans 1 and 3 each produce a $15,000 gain in 2026
None of the plans; the gain arises from the liability decrease and is $15,000 under any of them
items.rule_line: A partner's basis is increased by income and contributions and then decreased by distributions, including deemed cash distributions from liability decreases; distributions above basis cause gain, and only contributions made by year-end count.

why.A: Basis is measured at the end of the partnership's tax year. A contribution made after year-end cannot prevent gain for that year.
why.B: Forgets to increase basis by her $10,000 share of income. Distributions of $75,000 exceed basis of $60,000 by $15,000, not $25,000.
why.C: Basis is increased by income and contributions before it is reduced by distributions and the deemed distribution from the liability decrease. Before the contribution: $50,000 + $10,000 - $75,000 = -$15,000, so gain is $15,000. A December contribution of $20,000 brings basis to $5,000 and avoids gain. A January contribution comes too late for 2026.
why.D: Contributions increase basis, so a contribution before year-end can absorb the deemed distribution. The $20,000 more than covers the $15,000 shortfall.

steps: Basis before distributions = 50,000 + 10,000 = 60,000; distributions and deemed distribution = 40,000 + 35,000 = 75,000
Plan 3: contribution is in 2027, so the 2026 gain is 15,000

guide.ask: Which items raise basis before distributions are applied?
guide.reveal: Income and contributions: $50,000 + $10,000 = $60,000.

guide.ask: What reduces it?
guide.reveal: The $40,000 distribution and the $35,000 deemed distribution from the liability decrease, $75,000 in all, $15,000 more than basis before any contribution.

guide.ask: Which contribution timing fixes the shortfall?
guide.reveal: A contribution made within 2026, which raises basis to $80,000; one in January 2027 is too late.

items.task: Calculate the tax realized and recognized gain (loss) for both a partnership and partners on a nonliquidating distribution of noncash property, and the partner's basis in the property received.
items.stem: In 2023 Dev contributed land with a basis of $50,000 and a value of $200,000 to the DevCo partnership for an interest. The partnership still holds the land. In 2026 the partnership makes a nonliquidating distribution to Dev of other property worth $180,000, in which the partnership's basis is $90,000. Dev's basis in his partnership interest immediately before the distribution is $100,000, and no cash is distributed. The partnership could instead make the same distribution in 2031, when the land is still held. By how much does waiting until 2031 reduce the gain Dev recognizes?
items.rule_line: A partner who contributed appreciated property recognizes gain if the partnership distributes other property to him within seven years, equal to the lesser of the excess of the value received over his outside basis or his net precontribution gain.

why.A: Subtracts the built-in gain from the value received. The gain is measured by comparing the value received to his basis, not to the land's built-in gain.
why.B: This is the basis of the contributed land. The gain is measured by comparing the value received to his outside basis, and it is capped by the built-in gain.
why.C: A distribution to a contributing partner of other property within seven years of the contribution triggers gain equal to the lesser of the excess of the value received over his basis ($180,000 - $100,000 = $80,000) or his net precontribution gain ($150,000). Gain is $80,000 in 2026. In 2031, more than seven years have passed and a property distribution within his basis causes no gain.
why.D: This is the net precontribution gain, which is only a cap on the gain. The lesser amount, $80,000, is recognized.

steps: Excess of value received over outside basis = 180,000 - 100,000 = 80,000
Net precontribution gain = 200,000 - 50,000 = 150,000
2026 gain = min(80,000, 150,000) = 80,000; a 2031 distribution is outside the seven-year period and within his basis, so gain = 0
Reduction = 80,000
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 737(a), (b): lesser of excess of value over basis (reduced by money) or net precontribution gain; property contributed within 7 years.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group C / Nonliquidating distribution / Analysis

guide.ask: What limits the gain when the contributing partner receives other property within seven years?
guide.reveal: The lesser of the value received over his basis and his net precontribution gain.

guide.ask: Compute for 2026.
guide.reveal: $180,000 - $100,000 = $80,000, and net precontribution gain is $150,000, so the gain is $80,000.

guide.ask: What changes in 2031?
guide.reveal: The seven-year period has passed, and a distribution within basis produces no gain, so the reduction is $80,000.

items.task: Calculate the tax realized and recognized gain (loss) for both a partnership and partners on a liquidating distribution, and the partner's basis in the property received.
items.stem: Dina Voss, a general partner, retires from Voss & Klein, an accounting partnership in which capital is not a material income-producing factor. Her basis in her partnership interest is $100,000. In liquidation of her entire interest the partnership will pay her $300,000: $100,000 for her share of the partnership's cash and other property and $200,000 that reflects her share of unrecorded goodwill. Plan 1: the partnership agreement, which does not mention goodwill, stays as it is. Plan 2: the partners amend the agreement before Dina retires to provide for payment for her share of goodwill. Dina's rates are 37% on ordinary income and 20% on capital gain. The remaining partners are in the 37% bracket and receive any deduction the partnership gets. Ignore other taxes. By how much does Plan 2 increase the combined federal income tax of Dina and the remaining partners compared with Plan 1?
items.rule_line: In a service partnership, a retiring partner's payment for goodwill that the agreement does not mention is an ordinary income payment that the partnership deducts; if the agreement provides for goodwill it is a property payment taxed as capital gain, with no deduction.

why.A: This is the combined tax difference in Plan 1, where Dina's ordinary income is offset by the partners' deduction. Plan 2 adds capital gain tax with no offsetting deduction.
why.B: This is only Dina's tax saving from capital gain treatment ($34,000). It ignores that the partnership loses its $200,000 deduction.
why.C: Plan 1: the $200,000 for goodwill is a payment under the ordinary income rules, taxed to Dina at 37% ($74,000) and deducted by the partnership, saving the remaining partners $74,000, for a net of $0. Plan 2: the payment is a distribution for her interest, so she has $200,000 of capital gain ($40,000) and no deduction is available. Plan 2 increases combined tax by $40,000.
why.D: This is the value of the deduction lost by the remaining partners, without the tax Dina saves. Combined, Dina's tax falls by $34,000.

steps: Plan 1: 200,000 is ordinary to Dina (74,000) and deductible by the partnership (saves 74,000); basis 100,000 is recovered by the 100,000 property payment
Plan 2: total payment 300,000 - basis 100,000 = 200,000 capital gain; tax = 200,000 x 20% = 40,000; no partnership deduction
Plan 1 combined = 74,000 - 74,000 = 0; Plan 2 combined = 40,000; increase = 40,000
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 736(b)(3): the goodwill exclusion applies only if capital is not a material income-producing factor and the retiree is a general partner; stem amended to say general partner.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group C / Liquidating distribution / Analysis

guide.ask: How is a payment for goodwill treated if the agreement is silent, in a service partnership?
guide.reveal: As an ordinary payment to a retiring partner, taxed to her as ordinary income and deductible by the partnership.

guide.ask: What does the amended agreement change?
guide.reveal: The payment becomes a distribution for her interest, so it is capital gain to her and not deductible.

guide.ask: Compare combined tax.
guide.reveal: Silent agreement: $74,000 paid by Dina, $74,000 saved by the others, net $0. Amended: 20% x $200,000 = $40,000 with no deduction, a $40,000 increase.

items.task: Calculate a trust's accounting income, distributable net income and taxable income, including the income distribution deduction.
items.stem: The Larch Trust is a complex trust with 2026 distributable net income of $50,000, all ordinary income. The trustee paid $10,000 to beneficiary Beth during 2026 and will pay her $30,000 more on February 20, 2027. The trust has no 2027 income. Assume the trust's taxable income is taxed at a flat 37%, Beth is taxed at a flat 22% in both years, and ignore the trust's exemption. The trustee is considering whether to elect to treat the February 2027 payment as made on the last day of 2026. How much combined federal income tax (trust and Beth) does the election save?
items.rule_line: A trustee can elect to treat distributions made within 65 days after year-end as made on the last day of the year, so that the amount is carried out to the beneficiary and deducted by the trust, limited to distributable net income not already distributed.

why.A: Without the election, the trust is taxed on $40,000 (income of $50,000 less the $10,000 paid), $14,800, and Beth on $10,000, $2,200: total $17,000. With the election, distributions for 2026 are $40,000, so the trust is taxed on $10,000 ($3,700) and Beth on $40,000 ($8,800): total $12,500. The savings are $4,500.
why.B: This is only the tax Beth pays on the extra $30,000. The trust saves more tax at 37% than Beth costs at 22%, and the net saving is what matters.
why.C: This is only the trust's tax saving. The election makes Beth taxable on the $30,000, which costs her $6,600.
why.D: This is the combined tax without the election ($17,000), not the amount saved by the election.

steps: No election: trust taxable = 50,000 - 10,000 = 40,000, tax = 14,800; Beth tax on 10,000 = 2,200; total 17,000
Election: distribution deduction = 10,000 + 30,000 = 40,000 (not above DNI 50,000); trust tax = 10,000 x 37% = 3,700; Beth tax = 40,000 x 22% = 8,800; total 12,500
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 663(b) 65-day election. The amount limit is in Reg. 1.663(b)-1 (not opened).
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group D / Trust DNI/taxable income / Analysis

guide.ask: What does the election for the February 2027 payment change?
guide.reveal: It lets the trust count the payment as a 2026 distribution.

guide.ask: What are the two outcomes?
guide.reveal: No election: trust taxed on $40,000 ($14,800) and Beth on $10,000 ($2,200), $17,000. Election: distribution deduction $40,000, trust tax $3,700, Beth's tax $8,800, $12,500.

guide.ask: Savings?

items.task: Recall the different types of unrelated business income for tax-exempt organizations for tax purposes.
items.stem: Cedar Hall, a tax-exempt museum organized as a corporation, buys an office building for $2,000,000 using $1,200,000 borrowed from a bank at 6% interest and its own reserves, and leases it to a for-profit tenant. The lease is not related to the museum's exempt purpose. The building's average adjusted basis for the year is $2,000,000. Annual rent is $220,000, and straight-line depreciation and other expenses directly connected with the building, not counting interest, total $60,000. Plan A: keep the loan outstanding all year. Plan B: on January 1, repay $600,000 of the loan using reserves that are not debt-financed, so average acquisition indebtedness for the year is $600,000 and interest for the year is $36,000. Cedar Hall is taxed at 21% on unrelated business taxable income and has the $1,000 specific deduction. How much less tax does Plan B produce than Plan A?
items.rule_line: Income from debt-financed property is unrelated business income in the proportion that average acquisition indebtedness bears to average adjusted basis, and directly connected deductions, including interest on the debt, are allowed in the same proportion.

why.A: Deducts all of the interest instead of the debt/basis percentage of it. Interest is one of the deductions that is allowed only in the same percentage as the income.
why.B: Unrelated debt-financed income is the net income from the property multiplied by average acquisition indebtedness over average adjusted basis, and the directly connected deductions, including interest on the acquisition debt, are allowed in the same proportion. Plan A: 60% x ($220,000 - $60,000 - $72,000) = $52,800, less $1,000, taxed at 21% is $10,878. Plan B: 30% x ($220,000 - $60,000 - $36,000) = $37,200, less $1,000, taxed at 21% is $7,602. The saving is $3,276.
why.C: Assumes that repaying half the debt halves the tax. The interest deduction also falls, and the percentage applies to a different net income, so the saving is smaller than half of Plan A's tax.
why.D: Leaves out the interest deduction. Interest on the acquisition debt is a directly connected deduction, allowed in the debt/basis percentage, and it is lower in Plan B.

items.law_note: Corrected 2026-09-29: Reg. 1.514(a)-1(a) allows interest on the acquisition debt as a directly connected deduction in the debt/basis percentage. The draft said interest was excluded; the stem now gives interest and the answer changed from $10,080 to $3,276 (position B unchanged).

guide.ask: How is debt-financed income determined?
guide.reveal: Net income from the property multiplied by average acquisition debt over average adjusted basis; interest is deducted in the same proportion.

guide.ask: Compute each plan.
Saving?

items.task: Recall the different types of unrelated business income for tax-exempt organizations for tax purposes.
items.stem: Harbor Arts Society, a charitable organization exempt from federal income tax, publishes a members' magazine on subjects related to its exempt purpose. For the year it has $90,000 of gross advertising income, $30,000 of costs directly connected with selling the advertising, $40,000 of circulation income, and $100,000 of readership costs (editorial and circulation costs). A sales campaign could raise advertising income by another $50,000 with no added costs. By how much would the campaign raise the society's unrelated business taxable income before the specific deduction?
items.rule_line: For an exempt organization's periodical, net advertising income is unrelated business income, reduced by readership costs only to the extent they exceed circulation income and only up to the net advertising income.

why.A: Assumes the readership costs continue to absorb the extra income. The deduction for readership costs above circulation income is capped at $60,000.
why.B: Deducts the entire $100,000 of readership costs. Circulation income of $40,000 offsets part of those costs, so only $60,000 is deductible against advertising.
why.C: Advertising is unrelated income. Readership costs are deductible against it only to the extent they exceed circulation income ($100,000 - $40,000 = $60,000), and no more than the net advertising income. Now: net advertising $60,000, deduction $60,000, UBTI $0. After: net advertising $110,000, deduction still $60,000, UBTI $50,000. The increase is $50,000.
why.D: Ignores the readership cost deduction entirely. Readership costs above circulation income are deductible against advertising income.

steps: Readership costs in excess of circulation income = 100,000 - 40,000 = 60,000
Now: net advertising = 90,000 - 30,000 = 60,000; deduction = min(60,000, 60,000) = 60,000; UBTI = 0
Increase = 50,000
items.law_note: Confirmed Reg. 1.512(a)-1(f)(2)(ii): if readership costs exceed circulation income, UBTI is total periodical income less total periodical costs (same result as the explanation).
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area II / Group E / UBI types / Analysis

guide.ask: Are readership costs fully deductible against advertising income?
guide.reveal: Only to the extent they exceed circulation income: $100,000 - $40,000 = $60,000, and no more than net advertising income.

guide.ask: What is UBTI now and after the campaign?
guide.reveal: Now: net advertising $60,000 less $60,000 = $0. After: net advertising $110,000 less $60,000 = $50,000.

items.group_name: Formation and liquidation of business entities
items.task: Derive the tax implications of entity selection and formation decisions across multiple entity types and compare the results.
items.stem: Mia Chen, single, will run a business that earns $400,000 a year before any compensation to her and before employer payroll tax. She compares three structures. S corporation: she takes a $150,000 salary and leaves the rest as S corporation income. C corporation: she takes a $150,000 salary and the corporation distributes all remaining after-tax profit as a qualified dividend. Partnership taxed business (or sole proprietorship): all $400,000 is self-employment earnings. Assume her ordinary rate is 35% on taxable income and qualified dividends are taxed at 23.8% including the net investment income tax, and the corporate rate is 21%. Payroll tax is only Medicare of 1.45% for the employer and 1.45% for the employee on wages; on self-employment earnings it is 2.9% on 92.35% of net earnings, half of which is deductible. Ignore Social Security tax and additional Medicare tax. The business is not a specified service business, has no employees other than Mia and no depreciable property, and her taxable income is high enough that the wage and property limits apply in full to the qualified business income deduction of 20%. What is the difference between the highest and second highest after-tax cash she keeps from the business?
items.rule_line: A pass-through with owner wages can get the 20% qualified business income deduction when the wage limit applies, while a partnership with no wages cannot, and a C corporation pays two levels of tax on distributed profit.

why.A: Gives the partnership the 20% qualified business income deduction. Without W-2 wages or property, the wage and property limit reduces that deduction to zero at her income level.
why.B: Compares the partnership with the C corporation. The S corporation, with its salary supporting the deduction, is the highest, so the comparison is between it and the partnership.
why.C: S corporation: employer Medicare $2,175, S income $247,825, qualified business income deduction $49,565 (under 50% of wages), taxable income $348,260, tax $121,891, so after-tax cash is $273,759. Partnership: self-employment tax $10,713, no deduction because there are no wages, tax $138,125, after-tax cash $251,162. C corporation: $244,511. The S corporation is highest, and it exceeds the partnership by $22,597.
why.D: Compares the S corporation with the C corporation. The partnership, at $251,162, is second highest, not the C corporation.

steps: Partnership: self-employment tax = 400,000 x 92.35% x 2.9% = 10,713; taxable income = 400,000 - 5,357 = 394,643; no deduction; tax = 138,125; after-tax cash = 251,162
C corporation: corporate tax = 21% x 247,825 = 52,043; dividend = 195,782; individual tax = 52,500 + 46,596; after-tax cash = 244,511
Highest S corporation 273,759 less second highest partnership 251,162 = 22,597
items.law_note: The 20% deduction and its wage limit for 2026 depend on P.L. 119-21 §70105 (deduction made permanent). Rates are stem assumptions. Confirmed 26 USC 199A(b)(2)(B) wage/UBIA limit and (b)(3)(B) phase-in range $75,000 ($150,000 joint).
