guide.ask: What does the S corporation structure leave after all taxes?
guide.reveal: Employer Medicare $2,175, S income $247,825, deduction limited to $49,565, taxable income $348,260, tax $121,891; after-tax cash $273,759.

guide.ask: What do the partnership form and the C corporation form leave?
guide.reveal: Partnership: self-employment tax $10,713, tax $138,125, cash $251,162. C corporation: cash $244,511.

guide.ask: Which two are highest, and what is the gap?
guide.reveal: S corporation and partnership: $273,759 - $251,162 = $22,597.

items.group_name: Formation and liquidation of business entities
items.task: Derive the tax implications of entity selection and formation decisions across multiple entity types and compare the results.
items.stem: Nell Ford is starting a business in which she will materially participate. It expects a $200,000 loss in Year 1 and $200,000 of income before any loss deduction in Year 2. Nell invests $120,000 and expects to have no other basis, and she has other income taxed at 35%. She can form an S corporation or a C corporation. The C corporation is taxed at 21% and can carry its Year 1 loss forward, deducting no more than 80% of Year 2 taxable income before the deduction. Ignore payroll tax, qualified business income deduction, and any tax on Year 2 income itself. How much greater is the cumulative federal income tax saving through Year 2 from the Year 1 loss with the S corporation than with the C corporation?
items.rule_line: An S corporation loss passes through to the shareholder subject to basis, with any excess carried forward, while a C corporation's loss is a carryforward limited to 80% of taxable income.

why.A: Assumes the full $200,000 is used at each entity's rate, ignoring the 80% limit for the C corporation. That gives a $28,000 difference.
why.B: This is the C corporation's saving in Year 2 ($33,600), not the excess of the S corporation's saving over it.
why.C: S corporation: only $120,000 of the loss is deductible in Year 1, up to her basis (saving $42,000); the other $80,000 is suspended and deducted in Year 2 after income raises her basis (saving $28,000). Total $70,000. C corporation: the loss carries to Year 2, where the 80% limit allows $160,000 (saving $33,600). Difference $36,400.
why.D: This is the S corporation's total saving and not the difference from the C corporation.

steps: S corporation Year 1: deductible loss = min(200,000, 120,000 basis) = 120,000; saving 120,000 x 35% = 42,000; suspended 80,000
S corporation Year 2: Year 2 income increases basis, so suspended 80,000 is deducted; saving 80,000 x 35% = 28,000; total 70,000
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area III / Group A / Entity selection/formation comparison / Analysis

guide.ask: How much of the Year 1 loss can the S corporation shareholder deduct?
guide.reveal: Only up to basis, $120,000, saving 35% x $120,000 = $42,000; $80,000 is suspended.

guide.ask: What happens in Year 2 under each structure?
guide.reveal: S: the suspended $80,000 is deducted once income raises basis, saving $28,000, total $70,000. C: the loss carries forward and the 80% limit allows $160,000, saving $33,600.

guide.ask: Difference?

items.task: Derive the tax implications to a shareholder and C corporation for a proposed transaction after formation of the corporation, including noncash property contributions and noncash property distributions.
items.stem: Orion Corp., a C corporation taxed at 21%, will pay its sole owner-employee $100,000 of its current pre-tax earnings, and the corporation's total cash cost is the same $100,000 either way. Option 1: pay a deductible bonus, where the corporation's cost includes its share of Medicare tax. Option 2: pay a dividend out of the earnings after corporate tax. The owner's ordinary rate is 37%. Qualified dividends are taxed at 20% plus a 3.8% net investment income tax. Medicare tax on wages is 1.45% for the employer and 1.45% for the employee, plus 0.9% additional Medicare tax on the employee; Social Security tax does not apply because the wage base is already exceeded. Which option produces less combined corporate and owner federal tax, and by how much?
options: The bonus, by about $452
The bonus, by about $2,802
The dividend, by about $3,417
The dividend, by about $415
items.rule_line: Compensation is deductible but bears payroll tax, while a dividend from a C corporation is taxed at the corporate level and then to the shareholder, so the two can cost nearly the same and payroll tax details matter.

why.A: Leaves out the employer's Medicare tax on the bonus, which is part of the $100,000 cost. That makes the bonus look cheaper than it is.
why.B: Counts only income tax at 37% on the bonus. Medicare tax on wages, including the 0.9% additional tax, is a real cost of the bonus.
why.C: Leaves out the 3.8% net investment income tax on the dividend, making the dividend look cheaper than it is.
why.D: Bonus: $100,000 of cost covers a $98,571 bonus and $1,429 of employer Medicare; the owner pays 37% + 1.45% + 0.9% = 39.35% on the bonus, $38,788, so total tax is $40,217. Dividend: corporate tax $21,000 plus 23.8% on the remaining $79,000 ($18,802), or $39,802. The dividend costs about $415 less.

steps: Bonus B: B + 1.45% x B = 100,000, so B = 98,571 and employer Medicare = 1,429
Dividend: corporate tax = 100,000 x 21% = 21,000; dividend = 79,000; owner tax = 79,000 x 23.8% = 18,802; total = 39,802
The dividend is about 415 lower

guide.ask: What bonus fits inside a $100,000 total cost that includes employer Medicare?
guide.reveal: The bonus B solves B + 1.45% x B = $100,000, so B = $98,571 and employer Medicare is $1,429.

guide.ask: What is the combined tax on the bonus path?
guide.reveal: Owner pays 37% + 1.45% + 0.9% = 39.35% on $98,571, $38,788, plus employer Medicare $1,429, about $40,217 in all.

guide.ask: What about the dividend path, and which is lower?
guide.reveal: Corporate tax $21,000 plus 23.8% x $79,000 = $18,802, total $39,802, about $415 less.

items.task: Derive the tax implications to a shareholder and S corporation for a proposed transaction after formation of the corporation, including noncash property contributions and distributions, and loans and repayment of loans from and to a shareholder.
items.stem: Sal Reed owns all of Reed Mills, Inc., an S corporation since its formation, with stock basis of $200,000 that equals the net basis of its assets. The corporation has no liabilities. A corporate buyer will pay $1,000,000 for all of the stock in a purchase that qualifies for a joint election that treats the purchase as a sale of the corporation's assets followed by a liquidation, and the buyer is willing to make it. The assets are worth $1,000,000. Of the $800,000 total gain, $150,000 would be ordinary income from depreciation recapture and the rest long-term capital gain. Sal's rates are 37% on ordinary income and 20% on long-term capital gain. How much more federal income tax does Sal pay if the election is made?
items.rule_line: An election to treat a stock sale as an asset sale passes the corporation's ordinary income items to the S shareholders, so the shareholder can pay more tax even though the total gain is unchanged.

why.A: Without the election, the sale is a $800,000 capital gain on stock, taxed at 20% ($160,000). With it, the S corporation's deemed asset sale passes through $150,000 of ordinary income and $650,000 of capital gain ($55,500 + $130,000 = $185,500), and the deemed liquidation adds no more gain because his basis rose by $800,000. The extra tax is $25,500.
why.B: Taxes the recapture at only 20%. The extra cost is the 17-point rate difference on the $150,000, or $25,500.
why.C: This is the whole tax on the recapture, not the extra tax. The same $150,000 would otherwise be taxed at 20% as part of the stock gain.
why.D: This is Sal's total tax with the election. The question asks for the increase over the $160,000 stock sale tax.

steps: Election: pass-through of 150,000 ordinary (37% = 55,500) and 650,000 capital gain (20% = 130,000) = 185,500; deemed liquidation: basis 200,000 + 800,000 = 1,000,000, no further gain

What happens with the joint election?
guide.reveal: The deemed asset sale passes through $150,000 ordinary (37%, $55,500) and $650,000 capital gain (20%, $130,000), $185,500; the deemed liquidation adds nothing since basis rose.

items.task: Derive the tax implications to a shareholder and S corporation for a proposed transaction after formation of the corporation, including noncash property contributions and distributions, and loans and repayment of loans from and to a shareholder.
items.stem: Leah Voss, single, owns all of an S corporation that will earn $300,000 in 2026 before any salary to her and before employer payroll tax. She can defend either of two salaries as reasonable: $60,000 or $120,000. Assume Social Security and Medicare tax total 7.65% for the employer and 7.65% for the employee on wages (both salaries are below the Social Security wage base), her ordinary rate is 35%, and the corporation's remaining income passes through to her. Her taxable income is high enough that the wage limit on the 20% qualified business income deduction applies in full, so that deduction is limited to 50% of the W-2 wages paid. Ignore state taxes and additional Medicare tax. How much more after-tax cash does Leah keep with the $60,000 salary than with the $120,000 salary?
items.rule_line: A lower S corporation salary saves payroll tax but also reduces the wages that support the qualified business income deduction, so the two effects must be netted.

why.A: With $60,000 of wages: employer tax $4,590, S income $235,410, deduction limited to $30,000 (50% of wages), taxable income $265,410, tax $92,894, after-tax cash $197,927. With $120,000: employer tax $9,180, S income $170,820, deduction $34,164, taxable income $256,656, tax $89,830, after-tax cash $191,810. The lower salary keeps $6,116 more.
why.B: Leaves out the qualified business income deduction. It is not the same under both salaries, so the payroll savings from the lower salary are partly offset by the wage limit.
why.C: This is only the extra payroll tax from the higher salary. The lower salary also loses part of the deduction and pushes more income into the 35% bracket, so the net benefit is smaller.
why.D: Ignores the wage limit and gives the full 20% deduction under both salaries. At $60,000 of wages the deduction is limited to $30,000, which reduces the benefit of the low salary.

steps: Salary 120,000: employer tax = 9,180; S income = 170,820; deduction = min(34,164, 60,000) = 34,164; taxable = 256,656; tax = 89,830; after-tax cash = 191,810
items.law_note: The 2026 qualified business income deduction relies on P.L. 119-21 §70105. Both salaries are assumed reasonable.

guide.reveal: Employer tax $9,180, S income $170,820, deduction $34,164, taxable income $256,656, tax $89,830, cash $191,810.

items.task: Derive the tax implications to a partner and partnership for a proposed transaction, including a contribution of noncash property, a nonliquidating distribution of noncash property or the sale of a partnership interest.
items.stem: Tom Baird is offered a 10% interest in Quill LLC, a partnership with no debt, for services and without a cash contribution. Plan 1: he receives a 10% capital interest, immediately vested, that would entitle him to $100,000 if the partnership liquidated on that day. Plan 2: he receives a 10% profits interest that would entitle him to nothing on an immediate liquidation, and it meets the safe harbor requirements. Three years later he sells his interest for $130,000. Assume his rate is 37% on ordinary income and 20% on long-term capital gain, no allocations of income occur, and ignore self-employment tax, the partnership's deduction, and other items. How much less total federal income tax does Tom pay under Plan 2 than under Plan 1 on the receipt and the sale together?
items.rule_line: A partnership interest received for services is taxed as compensation to the extent of its liquidation value, but a profits interest that meets the safe harbor is not taxed when received and has no basis.

why.A: This is the tax on the sale under Plan 1 ($6,000). It ignores the tax on the receipt of the capital interest.
why.B: Plan 1: receipt of a capital interest is compensation of $100,000 ($37,000), and his basis becomes $100,000, so the later gain is $30,000 ($6,000): total $43,000. Plan 2: the profits interest is not taxed on receipt and has no basis, so the whole $130,000 is capital gain ($26,000). The difference is $17,000.
why.C: This is only the tax on the receipt of the capital interest. Plan 2 also pays more tax on the sale because it has no basis.
why.D: This is the total under Plan 1 ($43,000), not the difference between the two plans.

steps: Plan 2: no tax on receipt; basis 0; gain = 130,000 x 20% = 26,000
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area III / Group D / Proposed partnership transaction / Analysis

guide.ask: How is a vested capital interest received for services taxed?
guide.reveal: As compensation at its value, $100,000 x 37% = $37,000, with basis of $100,000.

guide.ask: How is a safe-harbor profits interest taxed?
guide.reveal: Not on receipt, with zero basis.

guide.ask: Compare the totals over the sale.
guide.reveal: Capital interest: $37,000 + 20% x $30,000 = $43,000. Profits interest: 20% x $130,000 = $26,000. Difference $17,000.

items.task: Calculate the realized gain, recognized gain and deferred gain on like-kind property exchange and involuntary conversion transactions for tax purposes and the basis of the asset received as a result of the transactions.
items.stem: Ola Peretz exchanges investment land with a basis of $200,000 and a value of $700,000 for other investment land worth $700,000 (like-kind, no boot). Plan 1: she exchanges directly with her brother, who owns the other land and who gives up land with a basis of $500,000. Fourteen months later her brother sells the land he received from Ola to an unrelated buyer for $700,000. Plan 2: she exchanges through a qualified intermediary with an unrelated party, and that party sells Ola's former land 14 months later for $700,000. Assume no exception to the two-year rule applies. Which statement about the gain Ola recognizes on her exchange is correct?
options: Plan 1: no gain recognized; Plan 2: no gain recognized, because both exchanges are of like-kind property
Plan 1: $500,000 recognized in the year of her brother's sale; Plan 2: no gain recognized
Plan 1: $500,000 recognized in the year of the exchange; Plan 2: no gain recognized
Plan 1: $500,000 recognized in the year of her brother's sale; Plan 2: $500,000 recognized in the year of the exchange
items.rule_line: Gain deferred in a like-kind exchange with a related person is recognized if either party disposes of the property within two years, in the year of the disposition.

why.A: Being like-kind is not enough for the related party exchange. A disposition by the related party within two years triggers the deferred gain.
why.B: Ola's realized gain is $500,000 in both plans. If a related person disposes of the property received within two years, the deferral is lost and Ola recognizes the deferred gain in the year of the second disposition, so Plan 1 gives $500,000 in the year of the brother's sale. Plan 2 is an exchange with an unrelated party, so the sale by that party has no effect on Ola.
why.C: The gain is recognized when the related person disposes of the property (the year of the brother's sale), not on the exchange date. If the property were held two years, Ola would have kept the deferral.
why.D: An exchange through a qualified intermediary with an unrelated party is a normal like-kind exchange. The unrelated party's later sale does not affect Ola.

steps: Realized gain = 700,000 - 200,000 = 500,000 in both plans
Plan 1: related party exchange; brother's sale within 2 years (14 months) triggers recognition of 500,000 in that year
Plan 2: exchange with an unrelated party; later sale is irrelevant to Ola, so no gain is recognized
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 1031(f)(1), (2): recognition on the date of the disposition; exceptions (death, involuntary conversion, no tax avoidance purpose) excluded by the stem.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area IV / Group A / Like-kind exchange / involuntary conversion / Analysis

guide.ask: What is Ola's realized gain, and what does a related-party exchange add?
guide.reveal: $700,000 - $200,000 = $500,000; if a related person sells within two years, deferral is lost.

guide.ask: Which plan involves a related party?
guide.reveal: The exchange with her brother, so his sale at 14 months triggers recognition in that year; the unrelated exchange is unaffected.

items.task: Calculate the realized gain, recognized gain and deferred gain on like-kind property exchange and involuntary conversion transactions for tax purposes and the basis of the asset received as a result of the transactions.
items.stem: Lena Ortiz's husband died on March 10, 2025. They had owned their main home and lived in it for ten years, as joint tenants with rights of survivorship, and their combined basis in it was $200,000. Its value on the date of death was $600,000. Lena has not remarried and will not remarry. She can sell the home for a net amount realized of $800,000 either on March 5, 2027 or on March 20, 2027. Assume she has owned and lived in the home for two of the last five years at each date and that her husband's half was included in his estate. How much more gain does she recognize by selling on March 20, 2027 than on March 5, 2027?
items.rule_line: A surviving spouse who has not remarried may use the $500,000 exclusion on a sale within two years of the spouse's death, and only the $250,000 exclusion later; the deceased spouse's half of jointly held property gets a stepped-up basis.

why.A: Assumes the exclusion covers the gain on both dates. The $250,000 exclusion after two years is less than her $400,000 gain.
why.B: Only her husband's half of the home gets a stepped-up basis, so her basis is $100,000 + $300,000 = $400,000 and the gain is $400,000. A sale by March 10, 2027 (within two years of death) still allows the $500,000 exclusion, so no gain is taxable. A sale after that date allows only $250,000, leaving $150,000 taxable. The difference is $150,000.
why.C: This is the difference between the two exclusion limits. The extra gain recognized is limited to the gain that exceeds $250,000, which is smaller here.
why.D: This is her entire gain of $400,000. A sale on either date qualifies for some exclusion, so not all of it is recognized.

steps: Basis = 200,000 / 2 + 600,000 / 2 = 400,000 (only the husband's half is stepped up); gain = 800,000 - 400,000 = 400,000
March 5, 2027 is within two years of March 10, 2025: exclusion 500,000, taxable gain = 0
March 20, 2027 is after two years: exclusion 250,000, taxable gain = 400,000 - 250,000 = 150,000
Difference = 150,000
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 121(b)(4): sale not later than 2 years after the spouse's death, unmarried at sale.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area IV / Group A / Like-kind exchange / involuntary conversion / Analysis

guide.ask: What is Lena's basis after her husband's death?
What exclusion applies by sale date?
guide.reveal: $500,000 if sold within two years of death, $250,000 after.

items.group_name: Amount and character of gains and losses on asset disposition and netting process
items.task: Calculate the amount of gain recognized on an installment sale.
items.stem: Rae Bolt sold business equipment for $300,000. She bought it for $250,000 and has claimed $150,000 of depreciation, so its adjusted basis is $100,000. Plan 1: take the full $300,000 in the year of sale. Plan 2: take $60,000 in the year of sale and $60,000 in each of the next four years, using the installment method with adequate stated interest. Assume ordinary income is taxed at 35% and long-term capital gain at 20%, and ignore interest. How much less tax does Rae pay in the year of sale under Plan 2 than under Plan 1?
items.rule_line: On an installment sale, depreciation recapture is recognized in the year of sale, and only the remaining gain can be spread over the payments.

why.A: The gain is $200,000: $150,000 of depreciation recapture (ordinary) and $50,000 of long-term capital gain. Recapture income is recognized in the year of sale even on the installment method, and it is added to her basis for the installment computation. The remaining $50,000 gain is reported as payments come in: 50,000 / 300,000 x $60,000 = $10,000 in the year of sale. Plan 2 defers $40,000 of capital gain, saving $8,000.
why.B: Assumes that the deferred $40,000 is taxed at the ordinary rate. Recapture is not deferred; the deferred gain is the capital gain part, taxed at 20%.
why.C: Spreads the whole $200,000 gain by the 66.7% gross profit ratio and taxes the $40,000 reported in the year of sale as recapture income. Recapture must be recognized in full in the year of sale, and only the capital gain is spread.
why.D: This is the year-of-sale tax under Plan 1 ($62,500), not the difference between the plans.

steps: Plan 2: adjusted basis after recapture = 250,000; gross profit percentage = 50,000 / 300,000; year of sale gain = 60,000 x 50,000 / 300,000 = 10,000; tax = 52,500 + 2,000 = 54,500
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 453(i): recapture income recognized in the year of disposition; remaining gain by the installment method.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area IV / Group B / Installment sale gain / Analysis

guide.ask: What is the gain and how much is recaptured?
guide.reveal: $300,000 - $100,000 = $200,000; recapture is $150,000 ordinary, recognized in the year of sale, leaving $50,000 of capital gain.

guide.ask: How much capital gain is reported in the sale year on installments?
Compare the sale-year tax.
guide.reveal: Full sale: $62,500. Installment: $52,500 + $2,000 = $54,500. Difference $8,000.

items.group_name: Amount and character of gains and losses on asset disposition and netting process
items.task: Calculate the Section 1231 capital gain and Section 1231 ordinary loss recognized for tax purposes on the disposition of an asset used in a trade or business.
items.stem: Kurt Lund had a net loss of $30,000 from sales of business assets held more than a year in 2025 that he deducted as an ordinary loss, and he had no other such net losses or gains in the prior five years. In 2026 and 2027 he plans to sell two business assets held more than a year: Asset X at a $100,000 gain and Asset Y at a $70,000 loss. Plan 1: sell both in 2026. Plan 2: sell X in 2026 and Y in 2027. Plan 3: sell Y in 2026 and X in 2027. Assume he is in the 37% bracket on ordinary income in both years, long-term capital gain is taxed at 20%, and ignore later years. Which plan gives the lowest total federal tax for 2026 and 2027?
options: Plan 1, with total tax of $11,100
Plan 3, with a net total tax saving of $25,900
Plans 1 and 3 equally, each with total tax of $11,100, and both lower than Plan 2
Plan 2, with a net total tax saving of $800
items.rule_line: Net section 1231 gain is treated as ordinary income to the extent of net section 1231 losses in the prior five years that have not been recaptured, so the timing of gains and losses across years changes their character.

why.A: Plan 1 nets to a $30,000 gain, all of it ordinary because of the 2025 loss recapture, for $11,100. Plan 2 is lower.
why.B: The 2026 ordinary loss saves $25,900, but the loss adds to the nonrecaptured losses, so the 2027 gain of $100,000 is all ordinary and costs $37,000. Total tax is $11,100.
why.C: Plans 1 and 3 do give $11,100, but Plan 2 is lower because it turns $70,000 of gain into capital gain in 2026 and uses the 2027 loss as an ordinary deduction.
why.D: In 2026 the $100,000 net gain is $30,000 ordinary (recapture of the 2025 loss) and $70,000 capital gain: $11,100 + $14,000 = $25,100. In 2027 the $70,000 net loss is ordinary and saves $25,900. Net is a saving of $800, against $11,100 of tax in Plan 1.

steps: Plan 1: 2026 net gain 30,000, ordinary by recapture of the 2025 loss: tax = 30,000 x 37% = 11,100
Plan 3: 2026 net loss 70,000 saves 25,900; 2027 gain 100,000 is ordinary up to nonrecaptured losses 30,000 + 70,000 = 100,000: tax 37,000; total = 11,100
Lowest is Plan 2 (a net saving of 800)
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 1231(c): net gain is ordinary to the extent of nonrecaptured net losses of the 5 preceding years.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area IV / Group B / Section 1231 netting / Analysis

guide.ask: How are net gains treated when earlier net losses were ordinary?
guide.reveal: As ordinary income up to the nonrecaptured losses of the prior five years.

guide.ask: What are the results for selling both in 2026, and for selling the gain first?
guide.reveal: Both in 2026: net gain $30,000 ordinary, tax $11,100. Gain first: $30,000 ordinary and $70,000 capital gain, $25,100; then a 2027 loss of $70,000 saves $25,900, net saving $800.

guide.ask: What about selling the loss first?
guide.reveal: Saves $25,900 in 2026 but the 2027 gain of $100,000 is fully ordinary: net $11,100 tax. Lowest is the gain-first plan.

items.group_name: Related party transactions, including imputed interest
items.task: Calculate the direct and indirect ownership percentages of corporation stock or partnership interests to determine whether there are related parties for tax purposes.
items.stem: Nilo Corp. is an accrual-basis, calendar-year C corporation taxed at 21%. At December 31, 2026 it owes year-end bonuses that are fixed and unconditional: $60,000 to Mira, who owns 60% of its stock and uses the cash method, and $90,000 to employees who own no stock. Plan 1: pay all bonuses on February 15, 2027. Plan 2: pay Mira's bonus on December 28, 2026 and the other bonuses on February 15, 2027. How much lower is Nilo's 2026 federal income tax under Plan 2 than under Plan 1?
items.rule_line: An accrual-basis payer may deduct an amount owed to a related cash-basis person only when the payee includes it in income, so the 2 1/2 month rule for bonuses does not help with a more-than-50% shareholder.

why.A: Assumes all bonuses are deductible in 2026 if paid within 2 1/2 months. That rule does not apply to amounts owed to a related cash-basis person.
why.B: Bonuses to unrelated employees paid within 2 1/2 months after year-end are deductible in 2026. Mira owns more than 50%, so an amount owed to her is deductible only when she includes it in income; a February payment is deductible in 2027. Under Plan 1 the 2026 deduction is $90,000; under Plan 2 it is $150,000. The extra $60,000 deduction saves $12,600.
why.C: This is the value of the deduction for the unrelated employees, which is available under both plans.
why.D: This is the total 2026 tax reduction under Plan 2, not the difference. The $90,000 of unrelated bonuses is deductible in 2026 under both plans.

steps: Mira owns 60% (over 50%), so she is a related person
Plan 1: 2026 deduction = 90,000 (unrelated bonuses paid within 2 1/2 months); Mira's 60,000 is deductible in 2027
Extra deduction = 60,000; tax = 60,000 x 21% = 12,600
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 267(a)(2), (b)(2): payor deduction deferred to the payee's inclusion; applies to compensation.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area IV / Group C / Ownership percentage calc / Analysis

guide.ask: Which bonus is deductible in 2026 if paid within 2 1/2 months?
guide.reveal: The one to unrelated employees, $90,000.

guide.ask: What about Mira's bonus, and what does paying in December change?
guide.reveal: Mira owns more than 50% and uses the cash method, so it is deductible only when she includes it: paying in 2026 makes it deductible in 2026.

guide.ask: Compute.
guide.reveal: Extra deduction $60,000 x 21% = $12,600.

items.group_name: Related party transactions, including imputed interest
items.task: Calculate a taxpayer's gain or loss on a subsequent disposition of an asset to an unrelated third party that was previously purchased from a related party.
items.stem: Ann Kohl sells rental land with a basis of $100,000 to her daughter Beth for $500,000. Beth pays $100,000 at closing and gives a note for $400,000 payable in four equal annual installments, and Ann uses the installment method. Plan 1: Beth resells the land to an unrelated buyer for $550,000 in the same year. Plan 2: Beth resells it to an unrelated buyer for $550,000 after holding it for three years. How much more of Ann's gain is recognized in the year of the sale to Beth under Plan 1 than under Plan 2?
items.rule_line: If a related buyer resells installment property within two years, the seller treats the lesser of the resale amount realized or the total contract price, less payments received, as received at the resale, which accelerates the gain.

why.A: This is Ann's gain in the sale year under Plan 2 ($80,000), not the additional gain under Plan 1.
why.B: The gross profit percentage is $400,000 / $500,000 = 80%. Under Plan 2 only the $100,000 down payment is received in the sale year, so gain is $80,000. Under Plan 1, a resale by the related buyer within two years is treated as a payment to Ann of the lesser of the amount realized ($550,000) or the total contract price ($500,000), less payments already received: another $400,000, so all of the gain is recognized: 80% x $500,000 = $400,000. The difference is $320,000.
why.C: Uses the resale price of $550,000 as the deemed payment. The deemed payment is limited to the total contract price, $500,000, less the payments already received.
why.D: This is all of Ann's gain in the sale year under Plan 1. Under Plan 2 she already recognizes $80,000 in that year, so the additional gain is $320,000.

steps: Gross profit percentage = (500,000 - 100,000) / 500,000 = 80%
Plan 2: sale year payment 100,000, gain = 100,000 x 80% = 80,000
items.law_note: Confirmed 26 USC 453(e)(1), (2): amount realized on the second disposition within 2 years is treated as received.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area IV / Group C / Subsequent disposition to unrelated party / Analysis

guide.ask: What is the gross profit percentage, and what is the gain when only the down payment is received?
What does a quick resale by the related buyer do?
guide.reveal: It is treated as a payment to Ann of the smaller of the resale price and contract price, less amounts already received: $400,000 more, so all gain is recognized: 80% x $500,000 = $400,000.

guide.ask: Difference?
